reports.title: Audit Finding Report — Sudan Education Covid-19 Response Project (SECRP), Grant Agreement No. TF0B3339, For the Year Ended December 31, 2021
reports.publisher: National Audit Chamber (ديوان المراجعة القومي), Republic of the Sudan
reports.description: Sudan's National Audit Chamber (a national government auditing body, equivalent to an Auditor-General's office) itemizes named states and, within them, named localities with specific monetary figures/discrepancies, in its audit of a World Bank-financed education grant. Section 6-3 (p.12), state-level table: "State Amount Amounts paid to schools through Sahara Organization the difference ... Central Darfur 67,499,068.00 7,07686.00 420,382.00 North Darfur 239,436,197.00 238,423,859.00 1,012,338.00 West Darfur the 81,935,210.00 81,549,390.00 385,820.00 Total 388,870,475.00 387,051,935 1,818,540". Section 6-4 (p.12-13), locality-level finding: "Delisting documents were not submitted to the auditor for some schools in localities that were selected as a sample in the six states that were visited in violation of Article (289/1) of the Financial and Accounting Procedures Regulations for the year 2011. ... State Locality The number of local schools Schools providing removal documents / Norh Darfur Umm Kadada 98 8 ... Blue Nile Baw 40 5". Signed by Mohamed Elhafiz Nasr Mohamed Nasr, Deputy Auditor General, on the cover letter (p.1, dated "/ /2022"). NOTE ON HOSTING: this document is hosted on the World Bank's project-document server (documents1.worldbank.org) as disclosure for a Bank-financed grant, not on a Sudanese government domain — but the content is Sudan-government-authored (National Audit Chamber), not World Bank-authored, so it is treated as a primary Sudanese government source per this project's evidence rule, with the hosting caveat flagged explicitly. NOTE ON SCOPE: this is a project-specific school-grant audit, not a general state/locality budget document — it is the strongest available evidence this round of a national body naming specific sub-national units (states AND localities) with financial figures, but it does not amount to a full state or locality budget/finance publication. Context (non-primary, cited for orientation only, not as an evidence source): UNICEF's 'The Impact of Sudan's Armed Conflict on the Fiscal Situation and Service Delivery' (https://www.unicef.org/sudan/media/13276/file/The%20Impact%20of%20Sudan's%20Armed%20Conflict%20on%20the%20Fiscal%20Situation%20and%20Service%20Delivery.pdf) states federal-to-state transfers stopped since March 2023 ("the government has been unable to make any current transfers to the states since March 2023") and itself cites 'National Chamber of Accounts, states report of final accounts for 2022' and 'National Chamber of Accounts, states annual audited accounts 2021' as its sources — consistent with, though not independently verified against, this Audit Chamber document.
reports.cadence_note: Project-specific audit tied to a single World Bank grant's implementation period (FY2021); not a recurring annual publication in the way a national budget is.

reports.title: Interim National Constitution of the Republic of the Sudan (2005) — Part Nine, State Revenue and Fiscal Allocation Provisions
reports.description: HISTORICAL — LIKELY SUPERSEDED, included as a historical primary source only, not as current law. This is the pre-2011 text of Sudan's 2005 Interim National Constitution (it still contains 'Government of Southern Sudan' provisions, predating the 2011 secession of South Sudan). Sudan's constitutional order has since been superseded multiple times (2011 post-secession amendments; 2019 Constitutional Charter; suspended by the 2021 coup; further disrupted by the 2023 civil war and subsequent 2023-2025 Constitutional Charter instruments), and no currently-operative Sudanese constitutional or statutory text with a comparable numeric state-finance formula could be located this round (the 2019 Constitutional Charter's fiscal content is limited to budget-approval procedure, not a sharing formula). Quoted for its historical value in establishing that Sudan's founding federal law DID name a specific state revenue formula: Art. 192(5) (p.66-67), oil revenue: "At least two percent of oil revenue shall be allocated to the oil producing states in proportion to output produced in the state, without prejudice to the special arrangements of Abyei Area." Art. 195 (p.69), states' own revenue sources: "The states may legislate for raising revenue or collecting taxes from the following sources:- a. state land and property tax and royalties, b. service charges for state services, c. licences, d. state personal income tax, ... f. state share of oil revenue as is set out in Article 192(5) of this Constitution..." Art. 198 (p.71), oversight body: "A Fiscal and Financial Allocation and Monitoring Commission shall be established, to ensure transparency and fairness both in regard to the allocation of nationally collected funds to the Government of Southern Sudan and the states," composed in part of "all finance ministers in all states of the Sudan" (Art. 198(3)(c)).
reports.cadence_note: One-off foundational constitutional instrument (2005); status as current law is unconfirmed and considered doubtful — see HISTORICAL flag above.

_dropped.why: sd-mofep-budget-2026 (already in af-sudan.json) states the FY2026 budget commits to transferring states' shares 'according to the Resource-Sharing Law' (قانون قسمة الموارد) but does not name, number, date, or quote that law's text, so it cannot be confirmed to mean the 2005 Interim National Constitution's Art. 192/195/198 revenue provisions specifically (Sudan may have a separate statutory 'Resource-Sharing Law' distinct from the constitutional text, and the constitutional provisions are themselves flagged historical/likely superseded). No document found this round explicitly links the two by citation, so the tempting topical edge is left undrawn per the evidence rule requiring a documented textual basis.

Sudan's National Audit Chamber's own domain (audit.gov.sd) was checked at both https://audit.gov.sd/?lang=ar&page_id=3290 and https://audit.gov.sd/?lang=en — the fetch tool returned ROBOTS_DISALLOWED, and a direct curl attempt failed with 'Could not resolve host' (http) and 'CONNECT tunnel failed, response 502' (https). A Wayback Machine lookup (http://archive.org/wayback/available?url=audit.gov.sd) was also attempted and returned 429 Too Many Requests (not retried further). The Audit Chamber's own web presence appears currently unreachable, consistent with wartime infrastructure disruption in Sudan; sd-nac-secrp-audit-2021 (this round's minted node) was located only via the World Bank's mirror/disclosure copy, not the Chamber's own site.

_dropped.edge: sd-* -> US State Dept 2024 Fiscal Transparency Report (Sudan)
_dropped.why: https://www.state.gov/reports/2024-fiscal-transparency-report/sudan/ returned HTTP 200 but the body was a bot-block 'Technical Difficulties / Exception: forbidden' page (effectively inaccessible); it also failed via the WebFetch tool with ROBOTS_DISALLOWED. Even if accessible, this is a U.S. State Department report, not a Sudanese government primary source, so it would not qualify as a citable node or evidence_url under this project's rule regardless.

http://mof.gov.sd/en fetched successfully but contained only news items (e.g., agricultural development in Northern and River Nile states); no links to state/locality budget documents, Local Government Act text, or Fiscal and Financial Allocation and Monitoring Commission (FFAMC) materials were found.

https://www.fao.org/faolex/results/details/en/c/LEX-FAOC129003/ and .../LEX-FAOC201663/ returned 403 Client Error on direct fetch; follow-up search confirmed these are actually Kenya's and Ireland's Local Government Acts respectively, not Sudan's — false leads from an ambiguous FAOLEX search, not usable regardless of the fetch error.

https://manshurat.org/node/13261, titled 'قانون نظام الحكم المحلي رقم 43 لسنة 1979' (Local Government System Law No. 43 of 1979), fetched successfully but turned out on inspection to be Egypt's 1979 Local Government Law, not Sudan's — a false lead from an ambiguous Arabic-language legal aggregator that is not country-scoped in its URL structure.

https://ar.wikipedia.org/wiki/قانون_الحكم_المحلي_في_السودان returned URL_NOT_FOUND ('this domain is cache-only and cannot be fetched'); moot in any case since Wikipedia is excluded as a source by this project's evidence rule.
https://www.moj.gov.sd/files/download/166 (Sudan Ministry of Justice document repository) returned 500 Server Error.

No current or post-2011 codified 'Local Government Act' for Sudan (north) with accessible full English or Arabic text and a numeric state/locality finance formula could be located. Searches for 1998, 2003, and post-2019 versions returned only South Sudan's 2009 Local Government Act (a different country, wrong-target) or dead ends. This is the single biggest gap in the state/locality-tier branch: no currently-operative statutory revenue-sharing formula was found to pair with, or supersede, the 2005 constitution's Art. 192/195/198 provisions.

Neither the Central Bank of Sudan's nor the Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning's sites were found to publish any state-by-state budget breakdown this round — only the national-level aggregate documents already present in the corpus (sd-cbos-statistical-review-q4-2024, sd-mofep-budget-2026, sd-budget-2021-transfers).

_dropped.edge: sd-* -> UNICEF 'Impact of Sudan's Armed Conflict on the Fiscal Situation and Service Delivery'
_dropped.why: UNICEF (a UN agency, not a Sudanese government body) is not eligible as a primary/government evidence source or evidence_url under this project's rule, so no node was minted for it. Its content is nonetheless valuable orientation, cited in prose inside sd-nac-secrp-audit-2021's description above: it documents that federal-to-state fiscal transfers have been suspended since March 2023 ('the government has been unable to make any current transfers to the states since March 2023'), explaining why no current state/locality budget document exists to find, and it cites (without the dispatched agent being able to independently retrieve) 'National Chamber of Accounts, states report of final accounts for 2022/2021' — corroborating that Sudan's Audit Chamber does routinely produce named state-level annual accounts, consistent with sd-nac-secrp-audit-2021.
